title: A named transportation technology project reached operation after procurement and reporting delays, without yet proving better public service
source_unit: Seattle Department of Transportation SMART Stage One final implementation report for Last Mile Freight Curb Access
geography: Seattle, Washington; commercial-vehicle permitting and digital curb-management project

observations.period: SMART Stage One project; 2023–2025 implementation and final report

denominator.unit: named Seattle SMART Stage One project

federal_award.unit: U.S. dollars in SMART Stage One funding

digital_curb_inventory.unit: project milestone for a digital commercial-loading-place inventory

commercial_vehicle_permit_system.value: digital commercial-vehicle permit and curb-management system implemented

implementation_delay.value: procurement, deployment, survey, and camera-reporting milestones finished later than originally planned

public_service_effect.unit: missing delivery reliability, curb-user time, enforcement, access, price, safety, equity, and durable continuation outcomes

observations.method: Review of Seattle DOT's official final implementation report submitted to USDOT, retaining planned and actual milestone dates, procurement and technology problems, stakeholder-engagement limits, and implementation outputs as separate fields.
observations.uncertainty: The report is a grantee account of one Stage One project. It documents implementation and reported operation but does not provide a representative curb-user sample, independent performance audit, baseline-to-follow-up service comparison, enforcement data, user costs, or evidence that the system continued after the reporting period.
observations.subgroup: Seattle DOT, commercial-vehicle permit holders, local businesses, non-permit holders, delivery operators, and curb users in the project area; the report does not quantify each group's exposure or outcome.
observations.counterinterpretation: A completed digital inventory and operational infrastructure can be valuable institutional capacity or learning even when direct user benefits are not measured; later outreach or Stage Two work could change the practical result.

related_sources.claim: USDOT lists Seattle's $1,996,000 SMART project and links its final implementation report.
GAO provides the cross-program context on SMART awards, delays, and incomplete conversion to usable public service.

boundary: This record adds a named project from grant award through digital inventory, procurement, installation, operational infrastructure, and final reporting. It does not establish better freight movement, shorter curb-search time, fairer access, safety, affordability, enforcement, user acceptance, or durable public service.
